Southern chestnut-tailed antbird (Sciaphylax hemimelaena) nestlings, like those of many terrestrial thamnophilids, begin life at a relatively modest size, with an initial wet body mass of approximately 3.5 grams [Ww0 = approximately 3.5 grams] recorded soon after hatching. This value, which serves as a comparative basis for the species' early growth trajectory, aligns closely with measurements documented for the congeneric Willisornis poecilinotus. The hatchling emerges from eggs incubated at a stable temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a thermal regime that appears critical for proper embryonic development. Data from captive breeding records indicate that the incubation period, defined as the interval from oviposition to hatching, lasts 16 days [ab = 16 days] at this temperature at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. This relatively extended developmental period within the egg likely reflects a combination of the species' altricial mode of development and the energetic constraints imposed by its insectivorous diet, which may limit the rate at which parents can provision the incubating female during the attentive phases of incubation.

Under the sustained thermal conditions characteristic of this species' active metabolic phase, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a predictable series of post-hatching milestones unfolds. The transition from nest-bound dependency to independent locomotion begins with fledging, which occurs at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. At this point, the developing chick is able to leave the nest, though it remains reliant on parental provisioning for several additional weeks. In comparison with other antbird species of similar body size, this fledging age is relatively short, suggesting a high rate of somatic growth during the nestling period. The rapid development of flight feathers and the achievement of sufficient muscle mass to support short flights are likely energetically demanding, and the 40.2 °C ambient temperature under which these measurements were taken may facilitate a higher metabolic rate, thereby accelerating tissue deposition and maturation.

Sexual maturity in this species is attained following a period of juvenile growth and development that culminates in gonadal activation. Under the same thermal conditions that characterize the active adult phase, specifically 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], puberty is reached at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching]. This relatively rapid progression to reproductive competence, when viewed against the backdrop of a small body size, suggests that individuals allocate a substantial proportion of their early energy budget toward the development of reproductive organs. The attainment of puberty does not immediately translate into breeding activity, however, as first-year birds may delay reproduction while they establish territories and secure access to food resources. Field observations indicate that immature birds often retain partial juvenile plumage for several months after reaching gonadal maturity, which may function as a signal of subordinate status to older, territorial adults.

The age at which individuals engage in their first successful breeding attempt, or time since birth at first brood, is considerably later than the onset of puberty. At a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], first reproduction is documented to occur at 438 days after hatching [tR = 438 days after hatching]. This substantial delay between sexual maturity and actual breeding reflects the complex social structure of this antbird, as young birds must compete for high-quality territories within the forest understory before they can attract a mate and secure a nest site. The interval likely also allows for the completion of somatic growth and the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. Females, which bear the primary energetic burden of egg formation, are particularly constrained by food availability during this pre-breeding period.

Adult females of the southern chestnut-tailed antbird reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 16 grams [Wwi = approximately 16 grams], a body mass that places them among the smaller members of the Thamnophilidae. This asymptotic mass, documented from a series of adult females in breeding condition, is consistent with the bow reported in the literature ranging from 14.5 to 16.5 grams. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild, again under the active-phase temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is 8 years [am = 8 years]. This longevity is notable for a bird of this size, as small passerines often face high extrinsic mortality rates from predation and environmental stressors. The annual reproductive output, inferred from a combination of typical clutch size and nesting frequency, is 2 offspring per year [Ri = 2 offspring per year], with breeding females estimated to initiate approximately one successful nesting attempt annually [F_R_i = approximately one successful nesting attempt annually]. The resting metabolic rate measured under these conditions reaches a maximum of 45.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 45.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that provides insight into the species' baseline energetic demands during periods of active thermoregulation at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].
